title: The 90-Second Spiral Stopper
promise: Use this guide to design and agree your Spiral Stopper — a single, pre-consented signal you and your partner choose together before the next argument starts, so either of you can deploy it the moment a familiar escalation begins and the conversation has somewhere to go instead of where it always goes.

nextStep.body:
The Spiral Stopper gives you a pause. What comes after the pause — the real money conversation, the in-laws conversation, the one about how the weight of running this family lands — those need more than a signal to interrupt them. They need a new way of talking to each other that neither of you has had yet, because the old way is what built the loop in the first place.

The Repeating Argument Reset is a free next step that gives you and your partner a named diagnosis of the specific loop your arguments run on and a single agreed interruption you can both use — built from what is actually happening, not the edited version. Bring the real pattern. We'll work out what it is and what to do with it.

sections.body:
You are not failing to communicate. You are both running a conditioned sequence.

Here is what that means practically: by the time the conversation about the school schedule has been had fifteen or twenty times in the same way, both nervous systems have stopped treating it as a new conversation. They have catalogued it. The moment a familiar phrase lands — 'you always leave this to me', 'here we go again', or even a tone of voice — the body decides, before either of you has spoken a second sentence, that it knows where this ends. It skips the middle and goes straight to the defensive position the last twenty versions of this argument taught it to expect.

That is why you can watch it happen in real time and still not stop it. The sequence is faster than your intention.

What this means for the fix: you cannot interrupt a conditioned loop in the middle of the loop, with words invented mid-fight by one person. That move is already inside the argument and it becomes another move in the argument. The only interruption that works is one both people have already said yes to — agreed when you were both calm, not deployed as a surprise by the partner who remembered the technique.
sections.heading: Why you can see it happening and still can't stop it

sections.body:
Before you choose a signal, you need a shared, neutral name for the specific sequence you are both in — not a verdict on who started it, just a description of the shape.

Fill in the template below together, ideally on a Sunday evening or any moment that is not inside a difficult conversation. Write it down. Both of you keep a copy.

---
**Our Loop — fill in together**

The topic that most reliably starts it:
> ____________________________________________
_(e.g. money / the in-laws / school admin / the division of the mental load)_

The phrase or tone that signals it has started:
> ____________________________________________
_(e.g. 'you always…' / a particular sigh / one of us going quiet / 'fine, forget it')_

The position each of us moves to once it's running:
> Partner A moves to: ________________________
_(e.g. defending, explaining, over-justifying)_
> Partner B moves to: ________________________
_(e.g. withdrawing, going silent, escalating the stakes)_

Where it always ends:
> ____________________________________________
_(e.g. one of us leaves the room / we go quiet for two days / nothing gets resolved)_

---
You now have a shared name for the pattern — not a diagnosis of who is wrong, but a map you both drew. That shared map is the first act of co-operation this argument has had.
sections.heading: Step 1 — Name your loop before your next conversation

sections.body:
Your signal needs three qualities: it must be agreed in advance, it must be usable by either person, and it must not be a word that already lives inside the argument.

Pick one from the list below, or write your own in the same format.

---
**Signal options — circle or write one**

☐ **A word that belongs to neither of you** — a neutral noun you'd never say mid-fight. Examples couples have used: 'Broccoli.' 'Tuesday.' 'Penguin.' Absurd enough to land differently from everything else in the argument.

☐ **A hand signal** — one open palm, raised briefly. No words required. Useful if voice tone is already part of the loop.

☐ **A phrase that names the loop, not the person** — 'I think we're in it.' Said flat, without accusation. Either person can say it.

☐ **Our signal:** ______________________________

---
**The agreement that makes it work — read aloud together and both say yes:**

> 'Either of us can use [our signal] the moment we recognise the loop starting. When one of us uses it, we both agree to stop for ten minutes before continuing. The signal is not a win for the person who uses it. It is a pause we both own.'

---
Write the signal and the agreement on a single index card. Put it somewhere both of you will see it.
sections.heading: Step 2 — Choose your Spiral Stopper signal

sections.body:
The signal buys you ten minutes. That time only works if both of you know in advance what you are doing with it — otherwise the pause becomes a cold silence that the argument absorbs and continues.

Fill in this pause plan now, not in the moment.

---
**Our Pause Plan**

When the signal is used, we each go to a separate space for ten minutes. The spaces we'll use:
> Partner A: ________________________________
> Partner B: ________________________________

During the pause, the one thing I will do to regulate (not replay the argument):
> Partner A: ________________________________
_(e.g. walk outside, make a drink, put headphones on — anything that interrupts the replay loop in your own head)_
> Partner B: ________________________________

After ten minutes, the person who used the signal is responsible for starting the re-entry:
> We will re-enter with this sentence:
> 'I want to talk about [the actual topic]. Can we try again?'

If one of us isn't ready at ten minutes:
> We will say: 'I need [specific extra time]. I will come back at [time].'
_(Name the time. Leaving it open is how the pause becomes a standoff.)_

---
This plan removes the two decisions that most reliably restart the argument: 'what are we supposed to do now?' and 'are you ever going to come back?'
sections.heading: Step 3 — Agree what the ten-minute pause actually looks like

sections.body:
Getting your partner to engage with this without it becoming a proof-point in the existing argument is the hardest part, and it falls to you to open the door. Use the script below verbatim or very close to it. The framing matters: you are not presenting a technique you found, you are asking for something you both need.

---
**Swipe copy — say this, or send it as a message if that's easier**

> 'I've been thinking about the conversations we keep having about [topic] — the ones that end the same way every time. I don't want to keep having that one. I read something about couples agreeing a signal in advance, when they're calm, so either of them can use it when they can feel it starting. It's not about who's right. I just want us to have something we've both agreed to before we're already in it. Would you be up for spending fifteen minutes on it this week? I can show you what I was thinking.'

---
**What to do if they say 'I don't want to do an exercise':**

> 'Fair enough. Could we just agree on a word — one word, that either of us can say when we can feel it starting? That's it. Just a word we both pick now.'

---
This keeps the ask small enough to say yes to. A single agreed word is enough to begin. The full plan can follow once the signal exists.
sections.heading: The script for raising this with your partner — before the next argument

sections.body:
Once you have filled in Steps 1–3, transfer your answers here. This is the version you both keep.

---
**Our Spiral Stopper — Reference Card**

**Our loop topic:**
> ____________________________________________

**The signal that tells us we're in it:**
> ____________________________________________

**Our agreed Spiral Stopper signal:**
> ____________________________________________

**What the signal means:**
> Either of us can use it. It is a ten-minute pause, not a win.

**During the pause, I go to:**
> Partner A: _________________ Partner B: _________________

**The re-entry sentence:**
> 'I want to talk about [topic]. Can we try again?'

**If I need more than ten minutes, I say:**
> 'I need [time]. I'll come back at [clock time].'

---
**What this does not fix:**
The Spiral Stopper interrupts the escalation sequence. It does not resolve the underlying topic — the real money conversation, the in-laws pattern, the mental load. It gives you both a moment of pause where previously there was none. What you do with that moment is the next piece of work.

---
Pin this to the fridge, save it in a shared note, or keep it anywhere both of you will find it before the next conversation that matters.
sections.heading: The one-page reference card — print and keep
